title: Run the quality gates in CI on every pull request
description: No CI exists; pull requests have merged on local checks alone. Add a GitHub Actions workflow that runs the four quality gates (pytest, ruff check, ruff format --check, mypy) on every pull request and on pushes to main. Security posture: least-privilege token permissions, no secrets, actions pinned to full commit ids, and no third-party action where a GitHub-owned one or a plain command will do. Any action or tool the workflow brings in needs a row in docs/DEPENDENCIES.md.
acceptance_criteria: The workflow's own pull request shows the checks running and passing; a deliberately failing test on a scratch branch would fail the check; docs/DEPENDENCIES.md records what CI depends on.
close_reason: Workflow added in PR #7 (stacked on #6); checks passed on GitHub. Open point for the owner: uv below 0.13.4 carries advisory GHSA-hq85-5cpj-mr62 per the subagent; CI works around it with the system certificate store.

title: goodall doctor checks the env file and the shared env file
description:
## Parent

"Spec: goodall's foundations (settings files, runner gateway, terminal output)" (goodall-yjt.9). Read the spec, the ADRs it cites (0005, 0008 to 0012) and GLOSSARY.md before starting. Work test-first and outside-in, as AGENTS.md requires: every criterion below is checked through the program's entry point unless it says otherwise.

## What to build

Doctor checks the two env files. In the env file beside local settings, every line must be a variable name and a well-formed secret reference for the secrets manager that local settings name; a value that is anything else is treated as a possible raw secret, rejected with a message that says to paste the reference, and never shown. In the shared env file in the record repo, any variable whose name ends in `_KEY`, `_TOKEN` or `_SECRET` is refused. A variable name that appears in both files is an error naming it. A missing env file is fine when the eval uses no secrets.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An env file whose lines are all well-formed references passes.
- [ ] A line whose value is not a well-formed reference fails the check, names the variable and the line, and the value itself appears nowhere in goodall's output, in text or in `--json`.
- [ ] A secret-looking name in the shared env file fails its check with "move this to the env file as a reference".
- [ ] The same name in both files fails a check naming the variable.
- [ ] A missing env file passes with a note; a missing shared env file is reported as a warning with a next step.
- [ ] Comments and blank lines in either file are accepted; a line that is not `NAME=value` is reported with its line number.
- [ ] Quoted and unquoted values are both read.
close_reason: Implemented in PR #21 (stacked on #19); GitHub checks passed. goodall.env_files reader, goodall.secrets_manager reference checks, three Secrets checks; no line content is ever repeated in output.

title: goodall doctor checks that referenced secrets exist, without reading them
description:
## Parent

"Spec: goodall's foundations (settings files, runner gateway, terminal output)" (goodall-yjt.9). Read the spec, the ADRs it cites (0005, 0008 to 0012) and GLOSSARY.md before starting. Work test-first and outside-in, as AGENTS.md requires: every criterion below is checked through the program's entry point unless it says otherwise.

## What to build

Doctor asks the secrets manager whether each item the env file refers to exists, using an operation that returns no secret value. This introduces the secrets manager module, the one purpose-built module above the runner, and the runner's discard output mode for any command that might print a secret. When the secrets manager is not signed in, that is one failure and the per-reference checks are skipped. When a reference cannot be checked safely, doctor says "could not verify" instead of passing or failing it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] With the secrets manager scripted as signed in and every item present, the check passes.
- [ ] A reference to an item that does not exist fails, naming the variable and the reference (a reference is not a secret).
- [ ] With the secrets manager scripted as signed out, one check fails with the sign-in step and the item checks are skipped naming it.
- [ ] A reference that cannot be checked without revealing a value is reported as "could not verify", with a status distinct from pass and FAIL in both the report and `--json`.
- [ ] The test asserts that every command sent to the secrets manager used the discard output mode or returned no value field.
- [ ] No test reaches a real secrets manager; an unscripted secrets manager command fails the test.
- [ ] The commands' modules never build a secrets manager command line themselves; they call the secrets manager module.
close_reason: Implemented in PR #22 (stacked on #21); GitHub checks passed. Secrets manager module with check_signed_in and look_up_referenced_items; only value-free op commands; new 'unverified' status because a field's existence cannot be checked without reading the value. Nothing was run against a real 1Password.

title: goodall doctor checks the tools and the macOS user account
description:
## Parent

"Spec: goodall's foundations (settings files, runner gateway, terminal output)" (goodall-yjt.9). Read the spec, the ADRs it cites (0005, 0008 to 0012) and GLOSSARY.md before starting. Work test-first and outside-in, as AGENTS.md requires: every criterion below is checked through the program's entry point unless it says otherwise.

## What to build

Doctor gains the checks that need to run other programs: that `git`, `gh` and the secrets manager's command are installed, that this macOS user account is a standard one and not an administrator, and that the record repo folder is a git repository. This introduces the runner gateway. A caller passes a command and reads back a result; a missing program, a timeout and a non-zero exit are results the check turns into a message with a next step, never exceptions. Short commands get a ten-second default timeout. In tests, a fake runner scripts everything except `git`, which runs for real.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each required program that is missing produces one failed check naming the program and how to get it.
- [ ] An administrator account fails the account check with an explanation of why a standard account is required; a standard account passes.
- [ ] A record repo folder that is not a git repository fails its check; the test uses real git in a temporary folder.
- [ ] A scripted command that never finishes is reported as timed out within the timeout, and doctor still completes.
- [ ] A test that runs a command the fake runner was not told about fails with a message naming the command.
- [ ] The runner is the only module that starts other programs; a test or lint rule enforces it.
- [ ] The real runner has its own tests against harmless real programs: one that succeeds, one that exits non-zero, one that does not exist, and one that outlasts a short timeout.
- [ ] A fresh-interpreter test shows the runner imports nothing outside the standard library.
close_reason: Implemented in PR #19 (stacked on #18); GitHub checks passed. goodall.runner (Command, CommandResult, Runner, RealRunner), goodall.fake_runner.FakeRunner, tool/account/record-repo checks, and a lint rule banning subprocess outside the runner.

title: goodall doctor prints its first report
description:
## Parent

"Spec: goodall's foundations (settings files, runner gateway, terminal output)" (goodall-yjt.9). Read the spec, the ADRs it cites (0005, 0008 to 0012) and GLOSSARY.md before starting. Work test-first and outside-in, as AGENTS.md requires: every criterion below is checked through the program's entry point unless it says otherwise.

## What to build

`goodall doctor` stops being a stub. It runs the settings checks and prints a grouped report a contributor can read at a glance: local settings found and valid, eval config found and valid, contributor in the roster, main workstream known. A check that depends on a failed one is skipped and names the check it was waiting for, so one broken thing shows as one failure. Each failure and warning carries a next step. A final line counts passed, warnings, failed and skipped. `--json` gives the same results, because both are renderings of one list of result records. Doctor changes nothing on the machine.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] On a healthy setup every check passes, the summary says so, and the exit code is 0.
- [ ] With local settings missing, exactly one check fails, the checks that depend on it are shown as skipped naming it, and the exit code is 1.
- [ ] Every failed check and every warning has a next step.
- [ ] The words pass, FAIL, warn and skip are always printed; with colour off the report is still complete.
- [ ] The whole report at a fixed width, with colour off, matches an expected screen in a test.
- [ ] `goodall doctor --json` prints one JSON document containing a version, a summary of counts, and one entry per check with a stable id, group, status, detail, next step and what it was waiting for; its exit code matches the report's.
- [ ] No file is created or changed by running doctor.
close_reason: Implemented in PR #18 (stacked on #17); GitHub checks passed. Check framework (goodall.checks), seven settings checks, grouped report and --json from the same records; doctor proven read-only by tests.

title: goodall status reads the eval config and reports that no work block is active
description:
## Parent

"Spec: goodall's foundations (settings files, runner gateway, terminal output)" (goodall-yjt.9). Read the spec, the ADRs it cites (0005, 0008 to 0012) and GLOSSARY.md before starting. Work test-first and outside-in, as AGENTS.md requires: every criterion below is checked through the program's entry point unless it says otherwise.

## What to build

`goodall status` follows the whole chain: local settings, then the record repo, then the eval config inside it. It checks that this account's contributor is in the eval's roster and that their main workstream is one of the eval's workstreams. When everything is in order it reports the eval's name, who the contributor is, and that no work block is active (none can exist yet), as readable text or as `--json`.

The eval config holds: a schema version, the eval's name and description, the workstreams, the intervention categories, one block per contributor (id and display name), and one block per scope entry (a repository identity and path patterns).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] With valid settings and a valid eval config in a temporary record repo, `goodall status` prints the eval's name, the contributor's display name and "no work block is active", and exits 1 (exit 0 is reserved for an active work block).
- [ ] `goodall status --json` prints one JSON document with the same facts and the same exit code.
- [ ] A missing or unparseable eval config, an unknown key, and a newer schema version each produce a failure naming the file and the fix.
- [ ] A contributor id that is not in the roster produces a failure naming the id and the roster's ids.
- [ ] A main workstream that is not in the eval's workstreams produces a failure listing the valid ones.
- [ ] A scope entry that contains a local path instead of a repository identity is rejected with an explanation.
- [ ] An email address or a secret reference in the eval config is rejected.
close_reason: Implemented in PR #17 (stacked on #15); GitHub checks passed. eval_config reader with roster and workstream cross-checks; status reports the eval, the contributor and that no work block is active.

title: goodall status reads local settings and explains what is wrong with them
description:
## Parent

"Spec: goodall's foundations (settings files, runner gateway, terminal output)" (goodall-yjt.9). Read the spec, the ADRs it cites (0005, 0008 to 0012) and GLOSSARY.md before starting. Work test-first and outside-in, as AGENTS.md requires: every criterion below is checked through the program's entry point unless it says otherwise.

## What to build

When local settings exist, `goodall status` reads them and either moves on or explains exactly what is wrong. A contributor who made a typo by hand is told which file and which line; one who misspelled a key is told the key is unknown; one whose settings were written by a newer goodall is told to upgrade; one whose record repo folder does not exist is told so, with the path. Until the eval config is read (a later ticket), a valid local settings file ends in a clear message that the eval config could not be read yet.

Local settings hold: a schema version, the contributor id, the main workstream, the record repo folder, the log directory, and the secrets manager's name.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A local settings file that is not valid TOML produces a failure naming the file and the line.
- [ ] A missing required key and an unknown key are each reported by name.
- [ ] A schema version newer than this goodall understands produces a failure that says to upgrade goodall.
- [ ] A record repo folder that does not exist produces a failure showing the path as written.
- [ ] A leading `~` in a folder setting is understood as the account's home.
- [ ] An unreachable log directory is reported as "not recording", not as a crash.
- [ ] Every failure has the three parts (what, why, what next) and exit code 1.
- [ ] A separate test starts a fresh interpreter, imports the settings reader, and asserts that nothing outside the standard library was loaded.
close_reason: Implemented in PR #15 (stacked on #11); GitHub checks passed. File renamed to local-settings.toml; unreadable files handled; --json shape is now {work_block_active, failures: [...]}.

"Spec: goodall's foundations (settings files, runner gateway, terminal output)" (goodall-yjt.9). Read the spec, the ADRs it cites (0005, 0008 to 0012) and GLOSSARY.md before starting. Work test-first and outside-in, as AGENTS.md requires: every criterion below is checked through the program's entry point unless it says otherwise.

## What to build

On a macOS user account where goodall has never been set up, `goodall status` fails clearly instead of saying "not built yet". The contributor sees what happened (no local settings were found, and where goodall looked), why it matters, and what to do next (run `goodall onboard`). This is the first slice through three foundations at once: the program's entry point accepting a runner and a terminal module, the lookup of local settings at a fixed place in the account's home with one environment variable able to override that place, and the terminal module's failure layout.

- [ ] With the settings location pointed at an empty temporary folder, `goodall status` exits 1.
- [ ] The failure is written to standard error and has three parts: what happened, why, and what to do next, naming `goodall onboard`.
- [ ] Nothing is written to standard output, and no file is created.
- [ ] The override variable `GOODALL_CONFIG_DIR` decides where goodall looks; without it, goodall looks under the account's home.
- [ ] The entry point accepts a terminal module and a runner, defaulting to the real ones; the test passes a captured terminal and reads the screen back.
- [ ] Colour appears only when output is a terminal, and the message reads correctly with colour off.
- [ ] `goodall status --json` reports the same failure as one JSON document on standard output, with the same exit code.

title: Spec: goodall's foundations (settings files, runner gateway, terminal output)
description:
## Problem Statement

A contributor who installs goodall today gets a command whose every subcommand says "not built yet". Nothing can read an eval's settings, run another program safely, or tell the contributor what is wrong and what to do about it. Every feature that follows (work blocks, the prompt gate, capture, setup, the full diagnostic) needs the same three things underneath it, and none of them exists:

- a way to find and read the eval's settings from any folder, and to say clearly when they are missing or wrong;
- a single safe way to run other programs, where a secret can never be captured and a test can never reach the real world;
- a single way to print results and failures, the same for a person reading a terminal and for an agent reading `--json`.

## Solution

Build goodall's foundations and prove them end to end through commands a contributor can actually run.

- `goodall status` finds local settings, reads the eval config through them, and reports plainly. With no settings it fails with what happened, why, and what to do next.
- `goodall doctor` runs its first checks: local settings, the eval config, the env file, the shared env file, the required tools, and the standard (non-admin) macOS user account. It prints a grouped report, or the same results as `--json`.
- The work-block commands take their final names: `goodall start`, `goodall stop`, `goodall status`.

Behind those commands sit the three foundations: the settings files and their checks, the runner gateway with its fake, and the terminal output module. Later features use them without redesigning them.

## User Stories

Finding and reading settings

1. As a contributor, I want goodall to find my eval's settings from whatever folder I am in, so that I never have to be "in the right place" to use it.
2. As a contributor, I want a clear message when local settings do not exist yet, telling me to run `goodall onboard`, so that I know what to do on a fresh macOS user account.
3. As a contributor, I want a clear message when local settings point at a record repo folder that does not exist, so that I can fix the path instead of guessing.
4. As a contributor, I want a clear message naming the file and the line when a settings file cannot be parsed, so that I can correct a typo I made by hand.
5. As a contributor, I want goodall to tell me when my contributor id is not in the eval's roster, so that my records are never attributed to nobody.
6. As a contributor, I want goodall to tell me when my main workstream is not one of the eval's workstreams, so that a renamed workstream does not silently break my default.
7. As a contributor who edits `eval.toml` by hand, I want my comments and layout left alone when goodall adds something to it, so that the file stays mine to read.
8. As a contributor, I want unknown keys in a settings file reported, so that a misspelled key is not silently ignored.
9. As a contributor on an eval whose settings were written by a newer goodall, I want a message that says so, so that I upgrade instead of getting confusing errors.
10. As someone starting an eval, I want the eval config to hold only what is true for every contributor, so that I can share the record repo without sharing anything about my machine.
11. As someone publishing an eval, I want the eval config to contain no email addresses and no secret references, so that it can be released as it stands.

Secrets

12. As a contributor, I want the env file checked so that every line is a well-formed secret reference for my secrets manager, so that a key pasted by mistake is caught immediately.
13. As a contributor, I want a pasted raw key rejected with a message that tells me to paste the reference, and never echoed back, so that the mistake does not spread into my terminal history or a transcript.
14. As a contributor, I want a variable whose name ends in `_KEY`, `_TOKEN` or `_SECRET` refused in the shared env file, so that nobody commits a secret to the record repo.
15. As a contributor, I want an error when the same variable name appears in both env files, so that I always know which value a program receives.
16. As a contributor, I want goodall to check that a referenced item exists without ever reading its value, so that diagnosing my setup cannot expose a secret.
17. As a contributor, I want to be told "could not verify" when goodall cannot check an item safely, so that I never mistake "not checked" for "fine".
18. As a maintainer adding a second secrets manager later, I want one module to change, so that supporting it does not ripple through the commands.

Diagnosing

19. As a contributor, I want `goodall doctor` to change nothing on my machine, so that it is always safe to run first when something seems wrong.
20. As a contributor, I want each failed check to say what to do next, so that I can fix it without reading source code.
21. As a contributor, I want one broken thing to produce one failure, with the checks that depend on it marked as skipped and naming it, so that I fix the real cause first.
22. As a contributor, I want a one-line summary of how many checks passed, warned, failed and were skipped, so that I can see the state at a glance.
23. As a contributor, I want the report readable without colour, so that it works when copied into an issue or piped to a file.
24. As a contributor, I want a slow or missing program to be reported as such within seconds, so that the diagnostic never hangs.
25. As an agent working in the eval account, I want `goodall doctor --json` to give the same results as the report in a stable shape, so that I can act on them without parsing prose.
26. As an agent, I want `goodall status --json` and its exit code to tell me whether a work block is active, so that I can decide whether to proceed.

Commands and output

27. As a contributor, I want to type `goodall start`, `goodall stop` and `goodall status`, so that the commands I use every day are the shortest ones.
28. As a contributor, I want `goodall start` to use my main workstream unless I pass `--workstream`, so that most days need no argument.
29. As a contributor, I want every failure to say what happened, why, and what to do next, in the same layout, so that I learn to read goodall's errors once.
30. As a contributor, I want failures on standard error and results on standard output, so that I can redirect results to a file and still see problems.
31. As a contributor, I want goodall never to ask me a question in the terminal, so that a command never sits waiting for input I did not expect.
32. As a contributor, I want goodall to exit with a code that distinguishes success, an error, a usage mistake and a closed prompt gate, so that scripts and agents can tell them apart.

Building goodall

33. As a goodall developer, I want to test any command by handing it a fake runner and a captured terminal, so that an outside-in test needs no real programs and no real screen.
34. As a goodall developer, I want a test that runs an unscripted command to fail loudly, so that no test can reach the real secrets manager or `gh` by accident.
35. As a goodall developer, I want real `git` to run in tests inside temporary repositories, so that git's actual behaviour is what gets verified.
36. As a goodall developer, I want to point goodall at a throwaway settings folder with one environment variable, so that tests and my own development never touch a real home folder.
37. As a goodall developer writing a hook later, I want the settings reader, the runner and the plain refusal message to import only the standard library, so that the prompt gate stays fast.
38. As a goodall developer, I want a test that proves the hook path imports nothing third-party, so that the rule cannot erode unnoticed.
39. As a goodall developer, I want a program that outlives one command to be represented by a record I can save and later use to stop it, so that `goodall stop` can end what `goodall start` began.

## Implementation Decisions

Settings (ADRs 0008, 0009, 0010)

- One macOS user account holds one eval. Goodall finds it through local settings at a fixed place in the account's home folder; one environment variable, `GOODALL_CONFIG_DIR`, overrides that place and is honoured everywhere.
- The chain is local settings, then the record repo, then the eval config. Local settings never override the eval config; the two hold different keys.
- Four files, each with one job. The shapes below came from a prototype the owner reacted to; they are provisional and carry a schema version so they can change.

The eval config, in the record repo:

    schema_version = 1
    name = "goodall-pilot"
    description = "..."
    workstreams = ["engineering", "research", "go-to-market"]
    intervention_categories = ["policy-mandated", "infrastructure", "agent-limitation", "freely-delegable"]

    [[contributors]]
    id = "ada-lovelace"
    display_name = "Ada Lovelace"

    [[scope]]
    repository = "github.com/your-org/goodall-pilot-app"
    paths = ["**"]

Local settings, in the account's home:

    schema_version = 1
    contributor = "ada-lovelace"
    main_workstream = "research"
    record_repo = "~/evals/goodall-pilot-records"
    log_directory = "/Volumes/EvalLogs/goodall-pilot"
    secrets_manager = "1password"

The env file, beside local settings (references only):

    ANTHROPIC_API_KEY_ENGINEERING="op://Eval/anthropic-engineering/credential"

The shared env file, in the record repo (non-secret variables for launched programs; its contents are a guideline, not a fixed list):

    CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1
    OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=otlp
    OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=otlp
    OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=http/json

- A scope entry names a repository by identity (host, owner, name) plus path patterns. It never holds a local path.
- TOML is read with the standard library. Goodall writes new TOML files with a small writer of its own that covers only the shapes above. When it changes a file a person may have edited, it appends a block and never rewrites the file.
- Goodall does not track billing. A workstream's line in the env file only decides which credential a program is launched with. Any cost goodall shows is an estimate.
- A missing or unreadable local settings file is a failure that names `goodall onboard` as the next step. An unreachable log directory counts as "not recording".

Runner gateway (ADR 0011)

- One general runner module is the only code that starts other programs. A caller passes a command and receives a result record. Program not found, timed out and exited non-zero are results, never exceptions. The result offers a ready-made one-line description of any problem.
- Each command states what happens to its output: captured, discarded (for anything that might print a secret), or the terminal handed over to the program.
- Short commands default to a ten-second timeout, overridable per call. Handing over the terminal has no timeout.
- A program that outlives one goodall command is represented by a plain record that can be saved and later used to stop it.
- Goodall makes no network calls of its own.
- One secrets manager module sits above the runner. It can check that a referenced item exists without receiving a value, and can launch a program with secrets injected. It is the only purpose-built module over the runner. 1Password is its one implementation today.
- Retrying is the caller's decision, not the runner's.

Terminal output (ADR 0012)

- One UI module is the only code that prints. It is built on the standard library. It offers a heading, a paragraph, a check result, a table or list, a failure, and JSON output. It offers no way to ask a question.
- A command builds its results once as records. The terminal report and `--json` are two renderings of those records. A failure record is always what happened, why, and what to do next.
- Results go to standard output; failures go to standard error. In `--json` mode standard output carries exactly one JSON document.
- Colour is used only when output is a terminal and is never the only signal: the words pass, FAIL, warn and skip are always printed. Width is measured once and clamped; piped output is a fixed width.
- A separate plain refusal function, importing nothing beyond the standard library's basics, serves the hook path.

Commands

- The work-block commands are top-level: `goodall start` (optional `--workstream`, defaulting to the contributor's main workstream), `goodall stop`, `goodall status`. "Work block" replaces "session" in goodall's own wording; the exit-code name for a closed prompt gate changes to match.
- `goodall status` exits 0 when a work block is active and 1 when not. In this spec no work block can exist yet, so it reports "no work block is active", or the settings failure.
- Exit codes: 0 success, 1 error, 2 usage error, 3 the prompt gate is closed.
- The program's entry point accepts a runner and a UI module, defaulting to the real ones.

The first diagnostic checks, in dependency order: local settings found and valid; record repo folder exists and is a git repository; eval config found and valid; contributor in the roster; main workstream known; env file holds only references; shared env file has no secret-looking names and no name shared with the env file; required programs present (`git`, `gh`, the secrets manager's command); the macOS user account is standard, not an administrator; referenced secret items exist.

## Testing Decisions

- A good test drives goodall the way a contributor or a hook would and checks what they would observe: the exit code, the text on standard output and standard error, the JSON document, the files on disk. It does not assert on internal function calls.
- The primary seam is the program's entry point, given a fake runner and a captured terminal. It is the highest seam available, and the owner agreed it. Every user story above is testable there.
- Settings are tested with real files in a temporary folder, selected through `GOODALL_CONFIG_DIR`.
- The fake runner scripts everything except `git`, which runs for real in temporary repositories. A command that is neither scripted nor allowed through fails the test.
- The runner's real adapter gets its own small tests against harmless real programs: a command that succeeds, one that exits non-zero, one that is missing, one that outlasts a short timeout, and starting then stopping a background program.
- The terminal module is tested by comparing whole screens at a fixed width with colour off, plus one test with colour on. These screens are the contract a future replacement would have to pass.
- One test starts a fresh interpreter, imports the hook-path modules, and asserts that nothing third-party was loaded.
- Tests are written first and seen to fail, outermost first.
- Prior art in this repo: the command-surface tests for the stubs, and the merged-branch hook's tests, which run a script as a separate process against a real git repository with a fake `gh`.

## Out of Scope

- The setup page and `goodall onboard`, including applying an answers file. (Decided in ADR 0012; built under the onboarding issue.)
- Creating, ending or recording work blocks; the prompt gate's behaviour; hooks. This spec only names the commands and reports that no work block is active.
- The record repo's git operations: writing entries, committing, pushing.
- Transcript capture and the telemetry receiver.
- The remaining diagnostic checks (hooks installed, record repo remote and visibility, receiver health).
- Any secrets manager other than 1Password.
- Tracking or reporting billing.
- `journal`, `intervene`, `sync`, `logs`, `export`, `dry-run`, `teardown` and `release`, which stay as stubs.

## Further Notes

- Decisions and their reasoning are in ADRs 0005 and 0008 to 0012; vocabulary is in the glossary. The wayfinder map "Map: a spec for goodall's foundations" (goodall-xes) indexes the eight decision tickets, each holding its full resolution.
- This spec supersedes the earlier Foundations issues "Build runner and UI gateways with a fake runner" and "Define project config model". "Rename the work-block commands to goodall start, stop and status" (goodall-yjt.7) is part of this spec's scope.
- Three independently produced designs for each gateway were compared before these decisions were made; the summaries are on tickets goodall-xes.4 and goodall-xes.6.
- The settings-file shapes are provisional by the owner's instruction and should stay easy to revise.
- Any new dependency needs the owner's approval and a row in the dependency log. This spec needs none.
close_reason: All eight tickets implemented as stacked pull requests #8, #11, #15, #17, #18, #19, #21 and #22, each with GitHub checks passing; none reviewed by the owner yet. Deferred pieces are noted on their first callers.

title: What do the four settings files look like?
description:
## Question

Four files are now decided in principle: the eval config and the shared env file in the record repo, and local settings and the env file in the eval account's home (ADRs 0008, 0009, 0010). Draft a concrete example of each to react to, for a two-contributor eval with three workstreams, one of them on API-key billing: exact file names and locations, the TOML tables and field names for the eval config and local settings, the variable naming convention in .env (including how a per-workstream model API key is named), what .env.shared contains for Claude Code's telemetry, the final name of the environment variable that overrides the local settings location, and how goodall writes TOML given the standard library only reads it. The owner reacts; the agreed examples become the spec's schema section.
notes: The setup page mock (branch prototype/onboard-page) already proposes file names the owner has seen without objecting: eval.toml, CONSTRUCT.md and .env.shared in the record repo; ~/.config/goodall/local-settings.toml and ~/.config/goodall/.env; plus an answers file goodall-answers.toml with tables [eval], [contributor], [local], [secrets] and [secrets.references], and variable names like ANTHROPIC_API_KEY_<WORKSTREAM>. Treat these as the starting draft for this ticket, not as decided.
close_reason: Provisional shapes agreed for eval.toml, .env.shared, local-settings.toml and .env; billing is not tracked locally, only estimated; see the resolution comment.

comments.author: Luke Thomas
comments.text:
Resolved by prototype with the owner on 2026-11-16: concrete drafts of each file, reacted to question by question. The owner's standing caveat: these are PROVISIONAL and must stay easy to revise; schema_version is in both TOML files for that reason. No ADR for the shapes themselves; ADR 0009 and the glossary were amended for decision 4.

The agreed drafts (the asset for the spec's schema section):

eval.toml, in the record repo, shared:

    schema_version = 1
    name = "goodall-pilot"
    description = "Building a SaaS product to first recurring revenue with AI."
    workstreams = ["engineering", "research", "go-to-market"]
    intervention_categories = ["policy-mandated", "infrastructure", "agent-limitation", "freely-delegable"]

    [[contributors]]
    id = "ada-lovelace"
    display_name = "Ada Lovelace"

    [[contributors]]
    id = "grace-hopper"
    display_name = "Grace Hopper"

    [[scope]]
    repository = "github.com/your-org/goodall-pilot-app"
    paths = ["**"]

.env.shared, in the record repo, shared:

    CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1
    OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=otlp
    OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=otlp
    OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=http/json

~/.config/goodall/local-settings.toml:

    schema_version = 1
    contributor = "ada-lovelace"
    main_workstream = "research"
    record_repo = "~/evals/goodall-pilot-records"
    log_directory = "/Volumes/EvalLogs/goodall-pilot"
    secrets_manager = "1password"

~/.config/goodall/.env:

    ANTHROPIC_API_KEY_ENGINEERING="op://Eval/anthropic-engineering/credential"

Also: CONSTRUCT.md in the record repo; the answers file is goodall-answers.toml with tables [eval], [contributor], [local], [secrets], [secrets.references] and a one_time_code, as in the setup page mock.

Decisions:
1. File names and places as above. PROVISIONAL (owner).
2. Eval config shape: plain settings at the top, one [[contributors]] block per contributor, one [[scope]] block per scope entry.
3. A scope entry is a repository identity (host/owner/name, never a local path) plus path patterns; ["**"] is the whole repository.
4. The main workstream lives in local settings.
5. OWNER'S STEER on billing: goodall should NOT be overly concerned with tracking billing locally; it is a hard problem (discounts and so on). People check what they spent elsewhere. Where convenient, goodall provides an ESTIMATE. Consequences: there is no billing setting and no billing-mode field to maintain; the env file line for a workstream only decides which credential a program is launched with (a workstream with an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY_<WORKSTREAM> reference is launched with that key, one without is not); cost shown by goodall is an estimate, for example from the list-price cost figure in Claude Code's telemetry.
6. OWNER'S STEER on the shared env file: a GUIDELINE, not a rule, about what it holds. Starting content is the telemetry switches. For now the receiver's address is set by goodall itself (it is machine-specific) and the switches that put prompt and response text into telemetry stay off (transcripts already hold that text; telemetry carries email and account ids). The one hard rule remains ADR 0010's: secret-looking names are refused there.
7. The override variable is GOODALL_CONFIG_DIR.
8. Writing TOML: goodall writes new files with a small writer of its own covering only the shapes above; when changing a file a person may have edited (adding a contributor to eval.toml) it appends a block and never rewrites the file.

title: What is the work-block command called?
description:
## Question

The glossary settles on 'work block' for a logged stretch of one contributor's work and says to avoid 'session' for it, because 'Claude session' means one conversation with Claude Code. The command is currently 'goodall session start|end|status' and a constant is SESSION_GATE_CLOSED. Should the command be renamed (for example 'goodall block ...' or 'goodall work ...'), or should 'session' stay as the command word with the glossary recording that? Whatever is chosen is applied to the CLI help, constants, tests, AGENTS.md and open issues.
close_reason: Top-level 'goodall start --workstream <name>', 'goodall stop' and 'goodall status'; 'work block' replaces 'session' in goodall's vocabulary.

comments.author: Luke Thomas
comments.text:
Resolved by grilling with the owner on 2026-11-16. No ADR: a command name is easy to change before release and would not surprise a reader. No glossary change needed.

Decisions:
1. The work-block commands are top-level: 'goodall start', 'goodall stop', 'goodall status'. There is no 'session', 'block' or 'work' group. Owner: 'and anything else we add to that level'.
2. OWNER'S CHOICE, against my recommendation of 'end': the command is 'goodall stop'. No alias. The glossary's noun stays 'end' (a work block has a start and an end; 'inferred end'); 'stop' is the verb a person types.
3. OWNER'S CHOICE, against my recommendation of a positional word: the workstream is given with a flag, 'goodall start --workstream research'. With no flag, the work block uses the contributor's main workstream from setup.
4. 'goodall status' reports only on the work block (active or not, since when, which workstream), offers --json, and exits 0 when a block is active and 1 when not. Wider health stays with 'goodall doctor'.
5. 'Work block' replaces 'session' throughout goodall's own vocabulary; 'session' is left to mean a Claude session. The constant SESSION_GATE_CLOSED becomes PROMPT_GATE_CLOSED.

Implementation is the existing issue goodall-yjt.7, now updated with the exact list.

title: Does goodall adopt a terminal library or print plainly?
description:
## Question

All terminal input and output goes through one UI module (AGENTS.md invariant 9). Should that module be built on a third-party terminal library, or on the standard library alone with a library adopted later only if the onboarding wizard proves to need one? Decide using the provenance findings, the readability bar for researchers, and the rule that hook code can never import the library.
close_reason: No terminal library: setup questions move to a no-server page in the browser, the terminal only prints, built on the standard library. See ADR 0012.

comments.author: Luke Thomas
comments.text:
Resolved 2026-11-16, folded into the runner gateway exploration at the owner's request. Three Opus subagents designed the UI gateway on the standard library, on rich and on click; the owner then proposed asking setup questions in the browser. Recorded as ADR 0012 (docs/adr/0012-setup-happens-on-a-page-with-no-server.md); 'setup page' and 'answers file' added to GLOSSARY.md; AGENTS.md invariant 9 reworded.

Agreed by the owner:
1. OWNER'S IDEA: interactive setup happens on a page in the browser, and the owner preferred a page with NO local server behind it.
2. The terminal only prints; it never asks a question. Unattended setup passes an answers file to goodall onboard.
3. Terminal output uses the standard library only: no rich, no click. (rich has one effective maintainer since its company closed in 2025; click saves little once prompts leave the terminal; neither offers arrow-key selection or multi-line editing.)
4. One set of records behind every output: the terminal report and --json are two renderings; a failure is always what happened, why, and what to do next (settles a fog item).
5. The page: the checklist layout showing the whole journey (before this page, on this page, finish); starting an eval and joining one are different paths; ONE 'Finish setup' button, no choice of how to save.
6. With no server, the waiting 'goodall onboard' picks up the saved answers file (matched by a one-time code written into the page), applies it, and reports IN TERMINAL. The owner accepted the result appearing in Terminal, not on the page.
7. Look and feel: lightly themed on khaki, forest and binoculars; examples branded 'goodall-', never after a sponsor.

Assets: both mocks are on branch prototype/onboard-page (commit 837d33a, local, not pushed): prototypes/onboard-page/onboard-page.prototype.html (the chosen design) and three-variants.prototype.html (the first round). Provenance findings: branch research/terminal-library-provenance.

Known risks to carry into the build: the browser may save the file somewhere other than Downloads or ask first; the page cannot check that folders exist; the download step itself was not exercised in the mock.

title: Which terminal libraries could goodall adopt, and what is their provenance?
description:
## Question

Goodall's wizard and diagnostic need prompts, tables and readable failure output. Establish, from primary sources and dated today, the candidates and their facts for the dependency rule in docs/DEPENDENCIES.md: at least rich (the predecessor's choice, re-verify), questionary and prompt_toolkit (rejected by the predecessor, re-verify), and any other credible option; for each the maintainer or organisation, repository and activity, advisory history, licence, and direct and transitive dependency count. Also establish what the standard library alone can do (input(), getpass, textwrap, shutil.get_terminal_size, ANSI codes) and its limits on macOS terminals.
close_reason: Provenance facts gathered for five terminal libraries and the standard library; findings on branch research/terminal-library-provenance.

comments.author: Luke Thomas
comments.text:
Resolved by a research subagent (Claude Opus 5.5) on 2026-11-16. Full findings with source links: docs/research/terminal-library-provenance.md on branch research/terminal-library-provenance (commit 6cd7879; never merged, no pull request).

Gist, facts only:
- rich 15.0.0 (MIT): Textualize, the company behind it, closed in 2025; Will McGugan now maintains it essentially alone. 3 packages installed. No advisories on rich; one low-severity Pygments issue fixed in 7 days. Tables and typed prompts, no arrow-key selection.
- questionary 2.1.1 (MIT, marked Beta): one maintainer, no release in 15 months. 2 packages installed. Every prompt type, no tables.
- prompt_toolkit 3.0.53 (BSD-3): effectively one maintainer. 1 package installed. No advisories.
- click 8.5.1 (BSD-3): Pallets volunteer team, six public members, the most active candidate. Zero dependencies, no advisories. Prompt, confirm, hidden input, single-key read and an editor hand-off for multi-line text; no list selector, no tables.
- InquirerPy 0.3.4: one maintainer, no commits since 2022.
- Standard library: input(), getpass, shutil.get_terminal_size and tty/termios cover text, hidden input and single-key reads. textwrap counts characters not display columns and does not handle ANSI codes. No tables, no list selector, no colour API. On macOS readline may be libedit.
- Could not verify: dependency counts from a real resolve; PyPI owner lists for most packages; who else can release rich or prompt_toolkit; import-time figures other than rich's published ~18 ms.

title: How are secret references represented now that an equivalent secrets manager is allowed?
description:
## Question

ADR 0006 requires every credential to be a reference into 1Password or an equivalent secrets manager, resolved at the moment of use, with 1Password the only one supported today. The predecessor used a .env file of op:// references resolved by 'op run'. How should goodall represent a secret reference so that 1Password works now and another manager can be added without changing the format: keep .env with manager-specific reference strings, or name the manager and the reference separately? What must goodall be able to check about a reference without ever resolving it?
close_reason: Secret references live in a .env beside local settings (references only); the manager injects values so goodall never sees them; non-secret variables go in .env.shared in the record repo. See ADR 0010.

comments.author: Luke Thomas
comments.text:
Resolved by grilling with the owner on 2026-11-16, over four rounds. Recorded as ADR 0010 (docs/adr/0010-secrets-reach-programs-through-an-env-file-of-references.md); ADRs 0006 and 0009 amended; GLOSSARY.md gains secrets manager, secret reference, env file and shared env file.

Decisions, each agreed by the owner:
1. Goodall holds references only for secrets goodall itself uses (a model API key per workstream; later an admin key for usage reports). The work's other secrets stay with that work; the record repo's push credential is git's.
2. One secrets manager per eval account, named once in local settings; each reference is a plain string in that manager's format.
3. OWNER'S CHOICE, against my recommendation to drop it: references live in a .env file, because it is a dominant paradigm and a file whose job is obvious matters more than having fewer files.
4. When a secret is used, the secrets manager launches the program with the value in its environment; the value never passes through goodall. This is the test for an 'equivalent' manager (ADR 0006).
5. Goodall may check that a reference is well formed (anything else is rejected as a possible raw secret); goodall doctor may ask the manager whether the item exists using an operation that returns no value, else it reports 'could not verify'.
6. The env file lives at ~/.config/goodall/.env beside local settings, never in a repository.
7. Every value in the env file must be a secret reference; nothing else.
8. OWNER'S ADDITION: non-secret environment variables that launched programs expect go in a version-controlled sibling, .env.shared, in the record repo, shared by every contributor.
9. A variable whose name ends in _KEY, _TOKEN or _SECRET is refused in .env.shared and must be a reference in .env. The owner called this a selling point.
10. The same variable name in both files is an error.
11. No local plain env file for now; goodall derives machine-specific values from local settings.

So the four files are: eval config and .env.shared (record repo, shared); local settings and .env (account home, local).

title: What does the runner gateway's interface look like?
description:
## Question

All subprocess and network calls go through one runner module with a fake for tests (AGENTS.md invariant 9). Sketch the interface to react to: what a caller passes and gets back for a command, whether HTTP requests belong in the same gateway or a separate one, how timeouts are expressed, how a test scripts the fake's answers and asserts on what was called, and whether real git (which tests are allowed to use) goes through the gateway too. The predecessor had CommandRunner with run() and http_get(), a SubprocessRunner and a FakeRunner; say what to keep and what to change.
close_reason: Hybrid: one general runner with an output mode and saveable background records, plus one secrets manager module above it; no network calls. See ADR 0011.

comments.author: Luke Thomas
comments.text:
Resolved 2026-11-16 by design-it-twice: three Opus subagents each designed the runner gateway under a different constraint (minimal interface; common caller first; a port per external tool), then the owner agreed a hybrid. Recorded as ADR 0011 (docs/adr/0011-one-runner-gateway-and-no-network-calls.md).

Agreed by the owner:
1. One general runner seam: runner.run([...]) returns a result record; expected failures (program not found, timed out, exited non-zero) are returned, never raised; the result carries a ready-made one-line description of any problem.
2. Each command states an output mode: capture, discard (for anything that might print a secret), or hand over the terminal.
3. Background programs (the telemetry receiver) are a plain record that can be saved, so a later goodall command can stop them; a work block starts and ends in different invocations.
4. One purpose-built secrets manager module sits above the runner (existence check that returns no value; launch a program with secrets injected). No ports for the account check or GitHub.
5. Short commands default to a 10-second timeout, overridable per call. Handing over the terminal has no timeout.
6. No HTTP and no network calls of goodall's own: all three designs dropped it independently, because a direct GitHub call would put the token's value inside goodall (ADR 0010). gh does the check.
7. The 'one runner module' invariant stays; reworded only to say goodall makes no network calls.
8. Retry is the caller's decision. In tests the fake runner scripts everything except git, which runs for real; an unscripted command fails the test.
9. Tests hand the runner and the UI module to the program's entry point (settles the fog item about where tests take hold).

The three full designs are in this session's subagent reports; the hybrid above is what the spec should describe.

title: What is eval-wide and what is local to one machine?
description:
## Question

The record repo is shared by every contributor to an eval, so what it holds must be true for all of them. Some settings are true only for one machine or one person: which contributor am I, where is my log directory, where is my copy of the record repo. Which settings belong in the eval config in the record repo, which belong in a machine-local file, and can a secret reference ever appear in either?
close_reason: Split by one test (true for every contributor?): eval config is shared, local settings are per account and never override it; secret references are local only. See ADR 0009.

comments.author: Luke Thomas
comments.text:
Resolved by grilling with the owner on 2026-11-16. Recorded as ADR 0009 (docs/adr/0009-eval-config-is-shared-and-local-settings-are-not.md); GLOSSARY.md updated (contributor narrowed to a person, roster added, eval config, local settings and declared scope redefined).

Decisions, each agreed by the owner:
1. A contributor is always a person. Agents are not contributors; records identify them by model and tool, and actor labels distinguish their entries.
2. The eval config holds a roster (id and display name per contributor); local settings hold one of those ids, saying which contributor this macOS user account is.
3. The eval config holds exactly: the eval's name and description, the roster, workstreams, declared scope, intervention categories and a schema version. The construct stays its own file in the record repo.
4. The declared scope names repositories by identity (and paths inside them), never by a local filesystem path.
5. Secret references appear only in local settings, never in the eval config. Accepted cost: each contributor sets up their own references at onboarding.
6. The roster holds no email addresses; commit authorship in the record repo comes from git's own settings.
7. The record repo's remote lives only in git. Onboarding asks for the URL once; goodall stores it nowhere else.
8. Local settings never override the eval config. The two files hold different keys.
9. Machine facts (hostname, macOS version, goodall version, Claude Code version) are recorded on each work block automatically and configured in neither file.

So local settings hold: record repo location, log directory location, contributor id, and secret references.

title: How does goodall find an eval's config and log directory from any folder?
description:
## Question

A goodall command or a Claude Code hook can run from any working directory, in any repository the eval touches. Something must tell it where the record repo (which holds the eval config) and the log directory are. One eval account holds one eval. What is that something: a file at a fixed place in the account's home, an environment variable, a search upward from the working directory, or a combination, and what happens when it is missing or points somewhere that does not exist (for example an unmounted log volume)?
close_reason: One eval per macOS user account, found through local settings at a fixed place in the account's home; see ADR 0008.

comments.author: Luke Thomas
comments.text:
Resolved by grilling with the owner on 2026-11-16. Recorded as ADR 0008 (docs/adr/0008-one-eval-per-macos-user-account-found-through-local-settings.md); terms 'local settings' and 'macOS user account' added to GLOSSARY.md.

Decisions, each agreed by the owner:
1. One macOS user account holds exactly one eval. Two evals in one macOS user account is unsupported; two on one Mac is fine when each has its own macOS user account.
2. Discovery is one file at a fixed place in the account's home, under ~/.config/goodall/. Not an environment variable (not reliably present) and not an upward search (work happens in repos that are not the record repo).
3. One environment variable (working name GOODALL_CONFIG_DIR) may override that location and is honoured everywhere, including hooks, so tests and goodall's own development never touch a real home folder. It is the only override.
4. That file holds the local settings: where this account's record repo is, where its log directory is, and which contributor this account is. Everything else comes from the eval config in the record repo. The chain is local settings -> record repo -> eval config.
5. When local settings are missing or unreadable, the prompt gate refuses the prompt with the fix; ordinary commands fail with the same message and exit code 1.
6. When the log directory cannot be reached, that counts as not recording: no work block is reported active and the gate refuses.
7. The file's contents are called 'local settings' (avoid local config, machine config, pointer file).
8. Write 'macOS user account' in full, shortening to 'account' only where the same paragraph has already used the full term; avoid 'profile'.

Left for the spec: the file's exact name, and the final name of the override variable.

title: Map: a spec for goodall's foundations
description:
## Destination

A spec for goodall's foundations (the runner gateway, the UI gateway and the eval config model), ready to hand to `/to-tickets`. The spec supersedes the existing Foundations issues "Build runner and UI gateways with a fake runner" (goodall-yjt.3) and "Define project config model" (goodall-yjt.4), and settles "Align command and constant names with the glossary's 'work block' and 'prompt gate'" (goodall-yjt.7). Those three are blocked on this map until it closes.

## Notes

- Domain: goodall, a tool that records what a person and their AI agents each did during an open-world eval. Read `GLOSSARY.md` and the ADRs in `docs/adr/` first.
- Use the glossary's terms, and update `GLOSSARY.md` the moment a term settles (domain-modeling skill).
- Write an ADR only when a decision is hard to reverse, surprising without context, and the result of a real trade-off.
- Consult the codebase-design skill for the gateway tickets; they are interface design.
- Any new dependency needs the owner's approval and a row in `docs/DEPENDENCIES.md`.
- Code run by hooks imports only the standard library (ADR 0005).
- Settled while charting, 2026-11-16, by the owner: the eval config is written in TOML. Hooks must read at least the log directory location, so the format has to be one the standard library parses; that rules out YAML, and TOML was chosen over JSON.
- Research subagents may push `research/*` branches. They are never merged and get no pull request.
- This map plans. It ends when the spec can be written with nothing left to decide.

## Decisions so far

<!-- one line per closed ticket: [title](id): gist -->

- [Which terminal libraries could goodall adopt, and what is their provenance?](goodall-xes.5): every candidate with tables or list prompts has one effective maintainer (rich lost its company in 2025); click has a team and no dependencies but no tables or list selector; the standard library covers text, hidden input and single keys only. Findings on branch research/terminal-library-provenance.

- [How does goodall find an eval's config and log directory from any folder?](goodall-xes.1): one eval per macOS user account, found through local settings at a fixed place in the account's home (one override variable); a missing file or unreachable log directory closes the prompt gate. ADR 0008.

- [What is eval-wide and what is local to one machine?](goodall-xes.2): the eval config holds only what is true for every contributor (name, roster, workstreams, declared scope, intervention categories); local settings hold locations, the contributor id and secret references, and never override it. ADR 0009.

- [How are secret references represented now that an equivalent secrets manager is allowed?](goodall-xes.3): references live in a .env beside local settings (references only); the secrets manager injects values so goodall never sees them; non-secret variables go in .env.shared in the record repo. ADR 0010.

- [What does the runner gateway's interface look like?](goodall-xes.4): one general runner with an output mode and saveable background records, one secrets manager module above it, and no network calls of goodall's own. ADR 0011.

- [Does goodall adopt a terminal library or print plainly?](goodall-xes.6): no library; setup questions are asked on a no-server page in the browser, the terminal only prints (standard library), and one set of records feeds both the report and --json. ADR 0012. Mocks on branch prototype/onboard-page.

- [What is the work-block command called?](goodall-xes.7): top-level goodall start (with --workstream, defaulting to the main workstream), goodall stop and goodall status; 'work block' replaces 'session' in goodall's vocabulary.

- [What do the four settings files look like?](goodall-xes.8): provisional shapes for eval.toml, .env.shared, local-settings.toml and .env (drafts in the ticket); main workstream is local; billing is not tracked locally, only estimated; the shared env file's contents are a guideline; GOODALL_CONFIG_DIR overrides the location; goodall appends to edited TOML and never rewrites it.

- Destination reached 2026-11-16: the spec is published as "Spec: goodall's foundations (settings files, runner gateway, terminal output)" (goodall-yjt.9).

## Not yet specified

- Nothing at present. The two earlier items (how failures and --json relate, and where tests take hold of the program) were settled with the gateway tickets.

## Out of scope

- The open-source README (goodall-yjt.5): writing, and it depends on later epics.
- The record repo's git operations (write, commit, push): they belong to the Record repo epic (goodall-g1k).
- Building the setup page itself: it belongs to the onboarding issue (goodall-ayy.2). This map settles only that the terminal does not ask questions.
close_reason: Destination reached: all eight decision tickets resolved and the spec published as goodall-yjt.9.

title: Rename the work-block commands to goodall start, stop and status
description: Decided on wayfinder ticket goodall-xes.7 (2026-11-16). Replace the 'goodall session start|end|status' group with three top-level commands: 'goodall start' (optional '--workstream <name>', defaulting to the contributor's main workstream), 'goodall stop' and 'goodall status'. Rename the exit-code constant SESSION_GATE_CLOSED to PROMPT_GATE_CLOSED and its comment. Remove 'session' from goodall's own wording wherever a work block is meant: CLI help (including the dry-run help text, which says 'a full session'), module docstrings, tests (the planned-commands list and the group-help tests), AGENTS.md, and the titles and descriptions of open Beads issues that say 'goodall session ...'. 'Session' stays only where a Claude session is meant. The glossary's noun 'end' (as in 'inferred end') is unchanged.
acceptance_criteria: Start from failing tests: 'goodall start', 'goodall stop' and 'goodall status' are listed in help and run their stubs; 'goodall session' is an unknown command (exit 2); 'goodall start --workstream research' parses; exit_codes.PROMPT_GATE_CLOSED == 3 and SESSION_GATE_CLOSED no longer exists. A search of src, tests and AGENTS.md finds 'session' only in the phrase 'Claude session'.
notes: This rename is within the scope of the Foundations spec (goodall-yjt.9); when the spec is broken into tickets, fold this in or make it one of them.
close_reason: Implemented in PR #8 (stacked on the CI branch); GitHub checks passed. 'session' remains only in tests asserting the old names are gone, Claude Code's own SessionStart event names, and the Beads-managed AGENTS.md block.

title: Claude hooks that stop agents committing to a branch whose PR is merged
description: Luke's request 2026-11-16: in other projects agents added commits to branches just after he merged their PRs. Add project hooks so an agent learns the branch's merge status at session start and periodically, and is blocked from git commit and git push on a branch whose pull request is already merged, with instructions to start a new branch from the default branch.
acceptance_criteria: Outside-in tests drive the hook script with real hook input, a real git repo and a fake gh; a commit on a merged branch is refused with the fix; unmerged branches, main, and non-git commands pass; a gh failure fails open with a note.
close_reason: Hook script, tests, settings registration and AGENTS.md rule committed on branch claude/branch-merge-status-hooks (3 commits). Verified against real GitHub by pipe-test; not yet observed firing inside a live session (settings load at session start). Not pushed.

title: goodall export scout
description: Build an Inspect Scout transcript database: Claude sessions through Scout's own claude_code importer, plus goodall's work blocks, journal entries and interventions mapped to the matching Inspect event types or transcript metadata, with actor labels attached. inspect-ai and inspect-scout are an optional extra imported only here; needs dependency approval first.
acceptance_criteria: Scout can open the exported database and filter by work block, actor label and intervention category; capture works with the extra uninstalled.

title: Parse human actions from Claude Code transcripts

design:
TARGET REPO: meridianlabs-ai/inspect_swe (mapping code lives in src/inspect_swe/_claude_code/_events/; inspect_scout wraps it; fixture tests live in inspect_scout, so a PR likely touches both).

DRAFT ISSUE (for Luke to review, edit and file himself):

Title: Claude Code transcript import: record user interrupts and tool-use rejections as events

## Feature request

**Problem.** `_claude_code/_events` (used by inspect_scout's `claude_code()` source) records nothing for the human's actions in a session other than prompt text:

- Typed prompts become `ChatMessageUser` with no `source` (extraction.py L37-80, `extract_user_message`) and appear only inside a later `ModelEvent`'s input. `isMeta`/`userType` are not read, so typed prompts and injected text look the same.
- Interrupt markers ("[Request interrupted by user]") are kept as ordinary user text. No `InterruptEvent` is emitted.
- A rejected tool call becomes `ToolCallError(type="unknown")`, the same as any other tool failure (events.py L243-256). Feedback the user gave with the denial stays inside the error string.

/clear and compaction are already handled (`split_on_clear`, `CompactionEvent`).

**Why.** Analysing human-in-the-loop sessions needs to find where the person stepped in. Today that means pattern-matching message text against strings Claude Code may change.

**Proposal** (existing types only):
1. Rejection -> `ApprovalEvent(call=<ToolCall>, approver="human", decision="reject", explanation=<feedback or None>)` before the `ToolEvent`, with `ToolEvent.error.type="approval"`.
2. Interrupt -> `InterruptEvent(source="user_cancel", interrupted="tool_call" | "generate", interrupted_tool_call_id=...)`.
3. Typed prompts -> `ChatMessageUser(source=...)` for non-meta user entries.

Detection strings in one function, with fixture tests; unknown shapes fall back to current behaviour.

**Questions.**
- Is `ApprovalEvent` right for a rejection with no approval policy? Approvals aren't in the transcript, so only rejections would appear.
- Should `approver` be "human", with the person in `metadata["decided_by"]` as in inspect_ai#6520?
- Should typed prompts use `source="input"` or `"operator"`, or should they get an event of their own?
- Which repo should own this: here, or in inspect_scout, where the fixtures live?

I can implement this with fixture transcripts (interrupt, deny, deny with feedback) if accepted.

*Drafted with AI assistance (Claude Code); I've reviewed it and checked the references against main.*
